paragraphs.heading: Light from collisions
paragraphs.text: An aurora is a natural glow in the upper atmosphere, produced when charged particles from the Sun crash into atoms of air. Those impacts excite oxygen and nitrogen, and the excited gases then release light in colours such as green, red and purple. The light can take the form of curtains, rays or spirals, or flicker across the whole sky.

paragraphs.heading: Where the names come from
paragraphs.text: Arctic displays go by the name aurora borealis, or northern lights, while Antarctic ones are the aurora australis, or southern lights. Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn, who crossed the sky from east to west to announce the coming Sun. Boreas and Auster were the Greco-Roman gods of the north wind and the south wind. Galileo used the term aurora borealis in his writings of 1619, and Pierre Gassendi used it in 1649 to describe a display seen across France in 1621.

paragraphs.heading: How the Sun sets it off
paragraphs.text: Auroras begin with disturbances in Earth's magnetosphere. These are caused by faster solar wind streaming from coronal holes and coronal mass ejections. The disturbances bend the paths of charged particles, mostly electrons and protons, which then rain down into the upper atmosphere. There they ionize and excite the gases, and those gases give off light of many colours and shapes.

paragraphs.heading: Where to look
paragraphs.text: Auroras are seen most often in the auroral zone, a band about 6° of latitude wide centred on 67° north and south. The area showing an aurora at any moment is called the auroral oval, and the solar wind pushes it away from the geomagnetic pole, about 15° toward the noon side and 23° toward the midnight side. In the north, places such as Alaska, Canada, Iceland, Scandinavia and Russia see the northern lights. In the south, the lights show over Antarctica, Patagonia, New Zealand and southeastern Australia.

paragraphs.heading: Storms push it outward
paragraphs.text: A geomagnetic storm makes both ovals grow, so the lights reach places much farther from the poles. On rare occasions the northern lights have been seen as far south as the Mediterranean and the southern United States. In the Carrington Event, the biggest geomagnetic storm anyone has seen, auroras reached even the tropics. Big storms are most common at the peak of the 11-year sunspot cycle and in the three years that follow.

paragraphs.heading: Twins, forecasts and other worlds
paragraphs.text: The southern lights look almost the same as the northern lights and change at the same moment. NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center issues short-term forecasts of where the oval will be and how intense it will be, giving 30 to 90 minutes of warning. Auroras are not unique to Earth: other planets, brown dwarfs, comets and some moons have them too.
